content: The surgical removal of an inflamed appendix is one of the most commonly performed procedures in clinical practice. Traditionally, open appendectomy (OA) has been the standard treatment for acute appendicitis due to its established therapeutic efficacy. However, with advancements in minimally invasive techniques, laparoscopic appendectomy (LA) has emerged as an alternative approach. LA involves smaller incisions, which may result in reduced postoperative pain, a lower risk of wound infections, and a quicker return to normal activities. This review updates a previous analysis published in 2010 and aims to compare the benefits and risks of LA versus OA. To conduct this review, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, and Embase, as of February 9, 2018. They also reviewed ongoing and proposed studies from the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), ClinicalTrials.gov, and the EU Clinical Trials Register. Additionally, reference lists of identified studies and conference proceedings from endoscopic surgical societies were manually searched. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing LA and OA in both adults and children were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager 5, with Peto odds ratios (OR) calculated for rare outcomes and mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) used for continuous outcomes. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The review included 85 studies with a total of 9,765 participants, of which 8,520 were adults and 1,245 were children. Many studies had methodological limitations, with attrition bias due to incomplete outcome data being the most common issue. In adults, LA was associated with reduced pain intensity on the first postoperative day, with a mean reduction of 0.75 cm on a 10 cm visual analog scale (VAS) (MD -0.75, 95% CI -1.04 to -0.45; 20 RCTs; 2,421 participants; low-quality evidence). Wound infections were less frequent after LA compared to OA (Peto OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.51; 63 RCTs; 7,612 participants; moderate-quality evidence). However, the incidence of intra-abdominal abscesses was higher following LA (Peto OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.43; 53 RCTs; 6,677 participants; moderate-quality evidence). The length of hospital stay was reduced by approximately one day with LA (MD -0.96, 95% CI -1.23 to -0.70; 46 RCTs; 5,127 participants; low-quality evidence). Additionally, patients undergoing LA returned to normal activities about five days earlier than those undergoing OA (MD -4.97, 95% CI -6.77 to -3.16; 17 RCTs; 1,653 participants; low-quality evidence). Two studies reported improved quality of life scores after LA, but due to the use of different measurement scales, pooled estimates were not provided. One study used the SF-36 questionnaire two weeks postoperatively, while the other used the Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index at six weeks and six months postoperatively (both low-quality evidence). In children, no significant differences were observed in pain intensity on the first postoperative day (MD -0.80, 95% CI -1.65 to 0.05; 1 RCT; 61 participants; low-quality evidence), the incidence of intra-abdominal abscesses (Peto OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.24 to 1.22; 9 RCTs; 1,185 participants; low-quality evidence), or the time until return to normal activities (MD -0.50, 95% CI -1.30 to 0.30; 1 RCT; 383 participants; moderate-quality evidence). However, wound infections were significantly less frequent after LA (Peto OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.42; 10 RCTs; 1,245 participants; moderate-quality evidence), and the length of hospital stay was reduced by approximately 0.8 days (MD -0.81, 95% CI -1.01 to -0.62; 6 RCTs; 316 participants; low-quality evidence). None of the included studies reported quality of life outcomes in children. In conclusion, LA demonstrated several advantages over OA in adults, including reduced pain intensity on the first postoperative day, fewer wound infections, shorter hospital stays, and quicker return to normal activities. However, LA was associated with a higher risk of intra-abdominal abscesses. In children, LA was superior to OA in terms of reduced wound infections and shorter hospital stays, but no differences were observed in other outcomes. Quality of life improvements were reported in adults but not assessed in children. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, and some observed benefits of LA were of limited clinical significance. Future research with rigorous methodology is needed, particularly to evaluate quality of life outcomes in children.
